subject: Biology
title: Molecular Clocks
description: A fast breakdown of Molecular Clocks for builders.

hook.text: DNA mutates at a roughly steady rate. Scientists use this ticking to date when species diverged.

buildup.text: By counting DNA differences between two species, researchers estimate how long ago they shared an ancestor.

discovery.text: Molecular clocks dated the human-chimp split to about 6–7 million years ago—matching fossil evidence.

twist.text: Different genes mutate at different rates. Choosing the wrong clock gives wildly wrong dates.

climax.text: Molecular clocks have rewritten evolutionary timelines for groups with poor fossil records.

punchline.text: DNA is a clock that never stops ticking.

quiz.question: How do molecular clocks estimate when species diverged?
options: By counting DNA mutation differences and their steady rate

details.summary: Molecular clocks use the steady rate at which neutral mutations accumulate in DNA to estimate when two species diverged from a common ancestor. By calibrating mutation rates against the fossil record, scientists can date evolutionary splits even when fossils are absent.
details.whyItMatters: Molecular clocks allow dating evolutionary events that left no fossil record, like the divergence of humans and great apes. They provide an independent timeline of evolution complementing and sometimes correcting dates from paleontology.
takeaways: Neutral mutations accumulate at relatively constant rates over time
Molecular clocks estimated human-chimp divergence at 6 to 7 million years ago
Clock rates vary between genes and lineages requiring careful calibration

faq.question: How accurate are molecular clocks?
faq.answer: Accuracy depends on calibration quality and whether mutation rates are truly constant. Rates can vary between lineages, genes, and over time. Modern methods use multiple genes and sophisticated models to account for rate variation, improving reliability significantly.

faq.question: Why do molecular clocks sometimes disagree with fossil dates?
faq.answer: Fossils record the earliest known occurrence of a species, not necessarily when it first appeared. Molecular clocks typically estimate earlier divergence times because the fossil record is incomplete. Both sources of evidence complement each other.
